plugins.name: api-client
plugins.description: Client data-fetching conventions: the shared apiFetch wrapper, typed responses, abortable requests, honest error surfaces.

skills.name: api-client
skills.title: api-client
skills.body:
# API client conventions

One fetch wrapper, typed responses, no ad-hoc fetch spaghetti.

---
## Rules

1. Use the project's apiFetch (it resolves the API base and same-origin semantics) — never bare fetch to relative paths.
2. Responses are parsed into declared interfaces; unknown shapes fail loudly at the parse, not three screens later.
3. Requests tied to unmounted components carry an AbortSignal; races on rapid input are cancelled, not debounced into mush.
4. Error UI states are explicit: loading, empty, error, retry — never an infinite spinner.
5. Polling intervals clean up on unmount and pause when the tab is hidden where practical.

plugins.name: ask-when-ambiguous
plugins.description: Ambiguity triggers one clarifying question, not a guess: irreversible or product-shaped decisions belong to the human.

skills.name: ask-when-ambiguous
skills.title: ask-when-ambiguous
skills.body:
# Ask when ambiguous

A wrong guess costs a rewrite; a question costs a minute.

---
## Rules

1. If two reasonable interpretations of the task lead to different deliverables, ask ONE concise question with your recommended default.
2. Irreversible actions (deleting data, force-pushing, schema drops, sending email) always get explicit confirmation first.
3. Product decisions (naming, UI copy, which of two features) belong to the human — propose, don't decide.
4. Reversible technical choices (algorithm details, internal naming) are yours — decide and note the choice.
5. When you proceed on an assumption, state the assumption prominently at the top of the summary.

plugins.name: auth-gates
plugins.description: Route handlers authenticate first: session checked before any work, per-user scoping on every query.

skills.name: auth-gates
skills.title: auth-gates
skills.body:
# Auth gates

Authentication is a precondition, not a feature.

---
## Rules

1. Every new route handler starts with the session check and returns 401 before touching data.
2. Scope every DB query by the authenticated user's id — never trust a userId from the request body.
3. Admin-only surfaces check the role/flag explicitly; absence of a UI is not access control.
4. Webhooks verify signatures before parsing payloads.
5. Idempotent side effects still require auth — replaying an authenticated action is not an auth bypass.

plugins.name: background-jobs
plugins.description: Long-running work follows the executor pattern: DB-backed state, lease/claim discipline, resumable progress, honest terminal states.

skills.name: background-jobs
skills.title: background-jobs
skills.body:
# Background jobs

Anything that can outlive a request needs durable state and a heartbeat.

---
## Rules

1. Job state lives in the DB (status + result columns), never only in process memory — restarts must not lose the trail.
2. Claiming uses atomic compare-and-swap leases so two workers cannot run one job.
3. Progress is written incrementally so the UI can show something honest while it runs.
4. Terminal states are explicit: completed, failed (with reason), cancelled — "stuck" is a bug to fix, not a status.
5. Startup reconciliation requeues jobs orphaned by a crash, bounded retries, then fails honestly.

plugins.name: backup-aware
plugins.description: Data-touching operations respect backups: snapshot before risky changes, verify restore paths, never hand-edit production data.

skills.name: backup-aware
skills.title: backup-aware
skills.body:
# Backup awareness

The backup you haven't tested is a wish, not a backup.

---
## Rules

1. Before bulk data operations (migration backfills, mass updates, deletes), confirm a recent backup exists and say so in the summary.
2. Prefer writing the new data alongside the old (dual-write / add-column-backfill) over in-place rewrites.
3. Practice restores, not just backups — the repo's restore drill script is the reference path.
4. Never hand-edit production data row by row; use a reviewed script that is idempotent and dry-runnable.
5. A failed data operation reports what state it left things in — partial progress is a fact to document, not hide.

plugins.name: branch-discipline
plugins.description: Feature-branch workflow guardrails: pushes to main/master are blocked, commits and pushes are announced, and every task starts from a clean tree.

skills.name: branch-discipline
skills.title: branch-discipline
skills.body:
# Branch discipline

main is releasable at all times; all agent work happens on branches.

---
## Rules

1. Check git status and the current branch before the first write. If the tree is dirty or you are on main, create/switch to a feature branch first (feat/<topic>, fix/<topic>).
2. One logical change per commit; rebase-style cleanups beat interleaved mega-commits.
3. Never push to main/master — open a branch and let the human merge after review.
4. If the repo has no remote, commit locally and say so; do not invent push commands.

plugins.name: ci-green
plugins.description: CI is the shared gatekeeper: the agent reproduces failing CI steps locally before pushing any fix.

skills.name: ci-green
skills.title: ci-green
skills.body:
# CI green

Pushing to 'see if CI passes' spends the team's time. Reproduce first.

---
## Rules

1. When CI fails, read the failing step's log and reproduce THAT exact command locally before changing any code.
2. Environment differences (env vars, DB, OS) are the first suspect — not the code.
3. Flaky tests get fixed or quarantined with an issue link, never ignored.
4. Never merge with a red pipeline; disabling a failing job is a team decision, not an agent decision.
5. After fixing, push and WATCH the pipeline to completion, then report the run link.

plugins.name: clean-imports
plugins.description: Import hygiene: no unused imports, no circular dependencies, consistent path aliases.

skills.name: clean-imports
skills.title: clean-imports
skills.body:
# Clean imports

The import graph is the architecture — keep it honest.

---
## Rules

1. Remove imports you no longer use in the same edit that stops using them.
2. Prefer the project's path alias (@/...) over fragile relative chains like ../../../.
3. Never introduce a circular dependency; if two modules need each other, extract the shared piece.
4. Type-only imports use "import type" where the bundler supports it.
5. Heavy optional dependencies load via dynamic import inside functions, not at module top-level.

plugins.name: conventional-commits
plugins.description: Commit messages follow Conventional Commits: type(scope): subject, imperative mood, body explains why.

skills.name: conventional-commits
skills.title: conventional-commits
skills.body:
# Conventional Commits

A commit message is addressed to the person bisecting a regression at 2am.

---
## Rules

1. Format: type(scope): subject — types: feat, fix, refactor, test, docs, chore, perf, build, ci.
2. Subject in imperative mood, ≤72 chars, no trailing period ("fix(auth): reject empty session tokens").
3. The body explains WHY the change exists and what tradeoffs were made; the diff already shows what.
4. Breaking changes get a "BREAKING CHANGE:" footer describing the migration.
5. One logical change per commit — if the subject needs "and", it wants to be two commits.

plugins.name: csrf-origin
plugins.description: State-changing endpoints verify origin/method semantics: JSON-only POSTs, origin checks, safe-method discipline.

skills.name: csrf-origin
skills.title: csrf-origin
skills.body:
# CSRF & origin discipline

A browser will happily send your cookies anywhere — verify who asked.

---
## Rules

1. State-changing JSON endpoints reject cross-origin requests (the app's proxy layer does this — do not bypass it with new middleware).
2. GET must stay side-effect free; anything that mutates is POST/PUT/DELETE.
3. SameSite cookie defaults are kept; do not switch cookies to SameSite=None without an explicit reason in the task.
4. Redirects validate destination URLs — open redirects are a vulnerability, not a convenience.
5. File downloads carry Content-Disposition and a fixed content type.

plugins.name: db-migrations
plugins.description: Schema changes are additive-first and pushed with the client regenerated — destructive steps are called out for human review.

skills.name: db-migrations
skills.title: db-migrations
skills.body:
# DB migrations

Production data is someone's day. Change schema like a surgeon.

---
## Rules

1. Prefer additive changes (new nullable columns, new tables) over destructive ones.
2. Any destructive step (drop column/table, type narrowing) requires explicit human approval in the task before pushing.
3. After schema edits: generate the client, push to the local dev DB, and run the typecheck lane — the ORM types must agree.
4. New query paths get indexes; say which query motivated each index.
5. Never edit an applied migration in place; add a new one.

plugins.name: dependency-audit
plugins.description: New dependencies are justified, pinned, and checked: no floating ranges, no packages that duplicate existing ones.

skills.name: dependency-audit
skills.title: dependency-audit
skills.body:
# Dependency audit

Every dependency is permanent maintenance — add them like it hurts.

---
## Rules

1. Before adding a package, check whether the repo already has one that does the job (bundlers ship a lot).
2. Pin with caret ranges only; never a bare latest, never a git URL without a commit.
3. Prefer tiny, focused, actively-maintained packages; note the weekly downloads and last publish when justifying.
4. After adding, run the install and the test suite — a dep that breaks the build does not get committed.
5. Record why the dependency exists in the task summary so removal later is easy.

plugins.name: doc-strings
plugins.description: Every exported function gets a doc comment: what it does, what it returns, and what it throws.

skills.name: doc-strings
skills.title: doc-strings
skills.body:
# Doc strings

Future readers include the agent in your next session — write for them.

---
## Rules

1. Every exported function/class/type gets a one-to-three line doc comment: WHAT it does, not how.
2. Document the non-obvious: surprising null returns, thrown errors, performance characteristics.
3. Never narrate the implementation in comments — explain intent and constraints ("because the API rate-limits at 8k/min").
4. Stale docs are worse than none: update the comment in the same edit that changes the behavior.
5. Module-level header comments state the module's responsibility in one sentence.

plugins.name: docker-hygiene
plugins.description: Containerfiles stay lean and reproducible: pinned bases, layered caching, non-root runtime user.

skills.name: docker-hygiene
skills.title: docker-hygiene
skills.body:
# Docker hygiene

Images are deployed artifacts — every layer is a liability you ship.

---
## Rules

1. Pin base images by digest or specific version tag — never :latest in anything deployed.
2. Order layers least→most volatile; copy lockfiles and install deps before copying source so builds cache.
3. One concern per container; multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the runtime image.
4. Run as a non-root user; expose only the ports actually used.
5. Healthchecks reflect real readiness (the app's own endpoint), not "process exists".

plugins.name: env-parity
plugins.description: Environment configuration stays explicit: new env vars are documented, defaulted, and never silently required.

skills.name: env-parity
skills.title: env-parity
skills.body:
# Env parity

Works on my machine is a configuration bug wearing a disguise.

---
## Rules

1. New env vars get: a safe local default, a .env.example entry with a comment, and a mention in the task summary.
2. Required-at-runtime vars fail loudly at startup with the variable NAME in the error — never a mysterious undefined downstream.
3. Secrets live only in secret stores/CI secrets — .env files with real values never get committed.
4. Prefer fewer, well-named variables over overlapping flags that can contradict each other.
5. Behavior differences between dev/prod are called out in the summary, not discovered later.

plugins.name: error-handling
plugins.description: Errors are typed, actionable, and never swallowed: no empty catch blocks, no string-only errors.

skills.name: error-handling
skills.title: error-handling
skills.body:
# Error handling

Every catch is a decision — make it deliberately.

---
## Rules

1. Never an empty catch. Either handle, wrap with context, or rethrow — and the choice is visible in a comment when subtle.
2. Catch specific errors, not everything. A broad catch belongs at the boundary (route handler, top of a task), not mid-logic.
3. Error messages say what failed, the offending value (truncated), and what to do about it.
4. User-facing messages never leak stack traces or internals; log the detail server-side.
5. Use the project's error hierarchy/types instead of bare strings.

plugins.name: evidence-summary
plugins.description: Task summaries cite evidence: exit codes, test names, file paths — claims are backed by shown output, not vibes.

skills.name: evidence-summary
skills.title: evidence-summary
skills.body:
# Evidence-based summaries

Show the receipt, then the claim.

---
## Rules

1. Every "done" claim carries its evidence: the command run and its exit code, or the test names that passed.
2. Summaries cite file paths with a one-line what/why for each — the user should be able to review in 60 seconds.
3. Unknowns and skipped steps are listed explicitly ("not verified: browser render, no dev server").
4. Numbers come from real output (build size, test counts) — never rounded from imagination.
5. No marketing adjectives in technical summaries ("robust", "comprehensive") — facts only.

plugins.name: form-validation
plugins.description: Form patterns: schema-driven validation shared between client and server, inline errors, disabled-while-pending submit.

skills.name: form-validation
skills.title: form-validation
skills.body:
# Form validation

The schema is the contract — write it once, use it on both sides.

---
## Rules

1. Define the zod schema once; the client validates for UX, the server re-validates for truth.
2. Validation errors render inline next to their field, with the message from the schema — not a generic toast.
3. Submit buttons disable while pending and show progress; double-submits are impossible by construction.
4. Server failures map back onto the form (field errors where identifiable) instead of vanishing.
5. Never trust pre-filled values from the URL/body — they pass through the same schema as fresh input.

plugins.name: input-validation
plugins.description: Every request body, query param, and external input is schema-validated before use — zod at the boundary.

skills.name: input-validation
skills.title: input-validation
skills.body:
# Input validation

The boundary is where trust ends — validate everything crossing it.

---
## Rules

1. Parse request bodies with a schema (zod) and reject with 400 + flattened issues on failure.
2. Validate query params and route params too — ids, pagination, enums — not just bodies.
3. Never interpolate raw input into shell commands, SQL, or HTML. Use parameterized APIs exclusively.
4. Length-cap and type-check strings before storing or echoing them.
5. External API responses get the same treatment: parse into a typed shape, assume nothing.

plugins.name: lint-clean
plugins.description: The linter is the gate: zero new warnings allowed, autofix first, disable-with-reason only when justified.

skills.name: lint-clean
skills.title: lint-clean
skills.body:
# Lint clean

Warnings rot into errors. The bar is exit 0 with --max-warnings 0.

---
## Rules

1. Run the project's linter after every edit batch; fix every new warning you introduced.
2. Prefer fixing the underlying issue over disabling the rule.
3. An inline disable must carry a reason and a scope as narrow as possible (next line, not the file).
4. Never reformat whole files when the project has no formatter config — match surrounding style instead.
5. Lint errors fail CI; treat them exactly like test failures.

plugins.name: log-hygiene
plugins.description: Logs are safe by construction: no tokens, no personal data, no full payloads — ids and summaries only.

skills.name: log-hygiene
skills.title: log-hygiene
skills.body:
# Log hygiene

Logs outlive the request and travel further than you think.

---
## Rules

1. Never log tokens, keys, passwords, cookies, or full authorization headers — log their presence, not their value.
2. Personal data (emails, names) is logged as ids unless debugging specifically requires it.
3. Truncate payloads to a bounded length; log shape ("received 42-item array") over content.
4. Use the project's logger with levels — console.log in committed code is a smell.
5. Errors log the stack server-side and a sanitized message to the client.

plugins.name: memory-saver
plugins.description: Durable workspace facts get captured: stack decisions, user preferences, verified patterns — so the next task starts smarter.

skills.name: memory-saver
skills.title: memory-saver
skills.body:
# Memory saver

The next session should not re-learn what this session paid for.

---
## Rules

1. When the user states a durable preference ("we use pnpm, never npm"), capture it via the memory capture path, not just this task's context.
2. Verified stack facts (which framework, which test runner) are worth remembering; one-off bug details are not.
3. Record decisions WITH their reason ("chose Zod — matches the other routes") so future changes can re-evaluate honestly.
4. Respect the cap: don't spam memory with per-task trivia; the retrieval layer boosts reinforced entries anyway.
5. When you see an existing memory contradicted by reality, correct it instead of working around it.

plugins.name: minimal-diff
plugins.description: Changes stay minimal and reviewable: no drive-by reformatting, no scope creep, every touched line justified by the task.

skills.name: minimal-diff
skills.title: minimal-diff
skills.body:
# Minimal diff

Review effort scales with diff size. Small diffs get real review; big diffs get rubber stamps.

---
## Rules

1. Touch only what the task requires. A drive-by cleanup is a separate task with its own commit.
2. Never reformat lines you are not otherwise changing — the diff must tell the story of the task.
3. Prefer editing existing files over creating parallel ones; prefer deleting code over adding abstraction.
4. If the honest fix needs a bigger change than the task allows, say so and stop — don't smuggle it in.
5. Summarize the diff shape at the end ("2 files, +40/−12, core change in X") so review starts oriented.

plugins.name: notification-events
plugins.description: App notification conventions: typed events into the notification center, user-readable copy, no raw errors.

skills.name: notification-events
skills.title: notification-events
skills.body:
# Notification events

Notifications are user-facing UI — write them like product copy, not logs.

---
## Rules

1. Long-running outcomes (run completed/failed, approval needed) emit into the notification center, not just console state.
2. Copy is specific: "Deploy of api-service failed — image build exited 1", never "Something went wrong".
3. Every notification carries a route/link target so clicking it lands somewhere useful.
4. Deduplicate repeat events for the same entity; aggregate storms ("3 files updated") instead of spamming.
5. Failure notifications include the first actionable fix, not just the error class.

plugins.name: path-containment
plugins.description: File operations stay inside the workspace: absolute-path escapes, traversal, and symlink hops are refused.

skills.name: path-containment
skills.title: path-containment
skills.body:
# Path containment

A path from outside the workspace is untrusted input.

---
## Rules

1. Resolve every user-supplied path and verify it is inside the workspace root before reading or writing.
2. Reject ".." traversal explicitly even after resolution — depth of defense, not cleverness.
3. Never follow symlinks out of the root; treat a symlinked escape as a hard error.
4. Relative paths in agent tools are resolved against the workspace, never the process cwd.
5. Log the refused path (truncated) when a containment check fails — it is a signal, not noise.

plugins.name: plan-then-act
plugins.description: Multi-step tasks get a visible plan first: steps enumerated, files identified, risks named — then execution follows the plan.

skills.name: plan-then-act
skills.title: plan-then-act
skills.body:
# Plan then act

Ten minutes of planning saves an hour of undoing.

---
## Rules

1. Any task touching more than ~3 files or 2 subsystems starts with a short written plan: steps, files, verification.
2. The plan names the riskiest step and how it will be verified — do that step's spike first if feasible.
3. Mid-task discoveries update the plan explicitly ("plan changed: X because Y") instead of silently drifting.
4. Do not plan what one search will answer — investigate first, plan only what stays unknown.
5. Finished steps get checked off in the summary so the user sees progress against the plan.

plugins.name: prisma-model
plugins.description: Prisma model conventions: cuid ids, timestamps, motivated indexes, snake_case table mapping, generate+push after edits.

skills.name: prisma-model
skills.title: prisma-model
skills.body:
# Prisma model scaffold

Conventions for new models in prisma/schema.prisma.

---
## Rules

1. Every model: id String @id @default(cuid()), createdAt DateTime @default(now()); add updatedAt when rows mutate.
2. Foreign keys get an @@index([fk]); every query path in the task gets an index — say which query motivated each one.
3. Map to snake_case plural tables: @@map("task_runs").
4. Json columns are for genuinely shape-flexible data; anything queried or filtered gets real columns.
5. After editing the schema: npx prisma generate (types) and npx prisma db push (local dev DB) — then run the typecheck lane.

plugins.name: react-component
plugins.description: React component conventions: hooks-first, props typed at the definition, lists keyed stably, effects narrow and cancellable.

skills.name: react-component
skills.title: react-component
skills.body:
# React component scaffold

Conventions for components in src/components.

---
## Rules

1. Props get a named interface at the top of the file; no anonymous inline object props on exported components.
2. State is the minimal truth — derive everything else during render instead of mirroring state.
3. Every effect has a cleanup for what it starts (subscriptions, timers, in-flight fetches with a cancelled flag).
4. Lists are keyed by stable data ids, never array indices that reorder.
5. "use client" only when the component truly needs it; server components are the default in app router.
6. Match the project's styling approach (this repo: Tailwind utilities + globals.css classes, theme-aware via .dark).

plugins.name: refactor-safety
plugins.description: Behavior-preserving refactors in small verified steps — never mix 'move code' and 'change behavior' in one edit.

skills.name: refactor-safety
skills.title: refactor-safety
skills.body:
# Refactor safety

Small steps, verified each time, beat heroic rewrites.

---
## Rules

1. One refactor = one commit = one behavior (which is: no behavior change). Mixing moves with changes makes review impossible.
2. Before moving code, run the suite; after moving it, run it again. Green to green or revert.
3. Rename by tooling where possible (find-all-references), never by search-and-replace across unrelated matches.
4. Delete dead code outright — commented-out code is noise, not safety.
5. Keep public APIs stable during internal refactors; deprecate loudly before removing.

plugins.name: release-notes
plugins.description: Every finished task produces a changelog-ready entry: what changed, why, migration/upgrade notes.

skills.name: release-notes
skills.title: release-notes
skills.body:
# Release notes

If it mattered enough to build, it matters enough to document in the changelog.

---
## Rules

1. End every feature/fix task with a one-to-three line changelog entry: what changed, who benefits, why.
2. User-visible changes lead; internal refactors get a single summary line or nothing.
3. Behavior changes and deprecations include an upgrade note ("set X=1 to keep the old behavior").
4. Match the repo's existing changelog format (Keep a Changelog / semantic versioning headers) when present.
5. Link the issue/PR id where the repo convention does.

plugins.description: Scaffolding for typed Next.js route handlers: auth first, zod-validated bodies, typed JSON errors, status-code discipline.

plugins.name: root-cause-first
plugins.description: Fix causes, not symptoms: reproduce, trace to origin, then patch — patching the nearest symptom is failure.

skills.name: root-cause-first
skills.title: root-cause-first
skills.body:
# Root cause first

A symptom patch is a bug with a delay timer.

---
## Rules

1. Reproduce the failure before fixing it; an unreproduced fix is a hypothesis, and hypotheses don't ship.
2. Trace the failure to its origin — the throwing line is rarely the broken invariant.
3. Prefer the small fix at the cause over the clever guard at the symptom; if you must guard, leave a comment linking the cause.
4. After fixing, explain the causal chain in one or two lines: "X happened because Y, so Z now fails".
5. If the same bug class has appeared twice in this workspace, fix the class (validation, typing), not the instance.

plugins.name: safe-commands
plugins.description: Shell commands run screened and narrow: no rm -rf, no curl|sh, no chained evasion forms.

skills.name: safe-commands
skills.title: safe-commands
skills.body:
# Safe commands

The shell is the most dangerous tool in the belt — treat it that way.

---
## Rules

1. Prefer argv-array process APIs over shell strings; when a shell is required, keep the command one line and quote variables.
2. Never pipe network input into an interpreter (curl | sh is always refused).
3. Destructive flags (-rf, --force, drop, truncate) need explicit user-visible justification in the task summary.
4. Prefer the project's own scripts (npm run ...) over ad-hoc command chains.
5. Long-running commands get timeouts; a hung process is a failure mode, handle it.

plugins.name: secret-hygiene
plugins.description: Blocks tool calls that would write or echo credential-shaped strings (AWS keys, GitHub tokens, private key blocks) before they land in any file or log.

skills.name: secret-hygiene
skills.title: secret-hygiene
skills.body:
# Secret hygiene

Credentials never belong in source, logs, or command output.

---
## Rules

1. Read secrets from environment variables or a secrets manager — never hardcode them, even "temporarily".
2. If you see a credential-shaped string in a diff or a file you are editing, stop and flag it to the user instead of preserving it.
3. Example/env files use placeholders (your-key-here), never real-looking values.
4. When a command might echo secrets (env, printenv, config dumps), prefer the narrow command that shows only what you need.

plugins.name: strict-types
plugins.description: No any, no silent casts: the agent must typecheck clean and prefer narrowing over assertions.

skills.name: strict-types
skills.title: strict-types
skills.body:
# Strict types

Types are the cheapest test you will ever write.

---
## Rules

1. No new "any" — including any[] and Record<string, any>. Use unknown and narrow.
2. Prefer type guards and discriminated unions over "as" assertions. Every "as" is a lie the compiler can't check.
3. Public function signatures are explicit — no inferred object soup on exports.
4. After edits run tsc --noEmit; zero new errors is the bar, not "it mostly compiles".
5. Null/undefined are handled at the boundary (validate input, then carry non-optional types inward).

plugins.name: test-first
plugins.description: Test-driven discipline: a failing test exists before any fix, and new features land with coverage.

skills.name: test-first
skills.title: test-first
skills.body:
# Test-first

A bug you can't reproduce in a test isn't fixed — it's postponed.

---
## Rules

1. For every bug fix, first write the smallest test that fails on the current code. Watch it fail. Then fix.
2. New features ship with at least one test per acceptance criterion.
3. Refactors run the existing suite before and after — green to green, no snapshot drift.
4. Never weaken an assertion to make a test pass. If the test is wrong, change the test and say why.
5. Prefer testing observable behavior over private internals.

plugins.name: token-frugality
plugins.description: Context-budget habits: read files in targeted slices, never re-read what is already in the transcript, prefer precise searches over dumps.

skills.name: token-frugality
skills.title: token-frugality
skills.body:
# Token frugality

Every token in the transcript is paid for on every later turn. Spend them on evidence, not bulk.

---
## Rules

1. Locate before you read: search for the symbol/pattern first, then read a window around the hit — not the whole file.
2. Never re-read a file whose contents are already in the conversation unless it changed since.
3. Prefer one precise search over three broad ones; prefer reading 80 lines around a match over 800 lines of context.
4. When a file must be edited in several places, batch the edits in one pass instead of re-reading between each.
5. Summaries you write are context too — keep them short, factual, and free of restated task text.

plugins.name: tool-budget
plugins.description: Deliberate tool use: every call has a purpose, redundant probes are batched, exploratory churn is visible and self-limited.

skills.name: tool-budget
skills.title: tool-budget
skills.body:
# Tool budget

Tools are for evidence, not for looking busy.

---
## Rules

1. Before each tool call, know what answer it will produce and what you'll do with it. If nothing changes either way, skip it.
2. Batch independent reads into one call; don't serialize what can be parallel.
3. A failed call is retried with a CHANGED approach — the same call twice expecting different output is churn.
4. Cap your own exploration: if you've made 5 calls without new information, stop and re-read what you have.
5. Long loops checkpoint progress (write the summary-so-far) so an interrupt doesn't lose the work.

plugins.name: verified-commits
plugins.description: The agent may only claim a task done when the machine agrees: typecheck and tests must exit 0 before any 'done' summary, and history rewriting is off-limits.

skills.name: verified-commits
skills.title: verified-commits
skills.body:
# Verified commits

Work is not done because the code looks right. It is done when the verification lanes pass.

---
## Rules

1. After every code change, run the project's checks (tsc --noEmit + the test suite) and read the EXIT CODES. Exit 0 is the only "passed".
2. Never summarize a task as complete while any check fails. Report the failure and the fix you attempted instead.
3. If a check was never run (no test suite, no compiler), say so explicitly — "unverified" is an honest status, a guess is not.
4. Never rewrite history: no git push --force, no git commit --no-verify, no amending commits you did not create in this session.
5. Commit small and often; every commit message says WHY, not just what.

plugins.name: ws-sse-streams
plugins.description: Streaming endpoint conventions: SSE with heartbeats, cursor-based resumption, client cleanup on unmount.

skills.name: ws-sse-streams
skills.title: ws-sse-streams
skills.body:
# SSE / streaming conventions

Streams leak — every one needs a close story.

---
## Rules

1. SSE responses set the right headers (text/event-stream, no-cache, keep-alive) and send an initial retry hint.
2. Heartbeats keep proxies from killing idle streams; the interval cleans up on close.
3. Event consumers are cursor-based: the client sends the last sequence, the server sends only what's newer.
4. Clients close EventSource/fetch-streams on unmount and on auth loss; reconnect is exponential-backoff, capped.
5. Payloads are JSON-stringified once at the server, parsed once at the client — no double-encoded nesting.
